# Introduction {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## Overview and learning goals

**Learn best practices for:**

- Organization and management of your research project files
- Documentation of your research project

. . .

<br>

::: callout-tip
### Two guiding principles [@noble2009]

1. Someone unfamiliar with your project should be able to look at your
   computer files and understand in detail what you did and why.
2. Everything you do, you will probably have to do over again.
:::

## Why does this matter?

Thoughtful and systematic project documentation and organization facilitates:

- Collaboration with others and your future self

. . .

- Reproducibility of your research

. . .

- Your ability to automate your work
- The use of use version control (week 4)
- Effective use of agentic AI (week 8)

# File organization and management {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## Recommended practices

1. Use one folder (folder hierarchy) for one project
2. Separate different kinds of files using a consistent subfolder structure
  
. . .

3. Avoid (manual) editing of your data and your results
4. Follow file and folder naming practices that favor machine- _and_
   human-readability
5. Use so-called "relative paths" to refer to files and folders within
   your project

Let's get into these!

## 1. Use one folder for one project

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}

- All files for one project should be contained in one folder
  hierarchy -- and make liberal use of subfolders!
- Don't scatter files from one project across your computer

. . .

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

**This makes it easier to:**

- Find files
- Share or back up your entire project
- Avoid throwing away stuff in error

. . .

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
See the [lecture notes](./w2b_project-org_page.qmd) for a discussion of how to handle
shared data or code between projects.
:::

:::
::: {.column width="55%"}

![](../img/proj-dirs-1-2025.svg){fig-align="center" width="95%" fig-alt="A diagram showing two research project folder hierarchies."}

::: legend2
Two project folder hierarchies. Each box is a folder.
:::

:::
:::

## 2. Separate files using a consistent structure

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}

Use subfolders to separate, for example:

- Code
- Data
- Results (of data processing and analysis)

:::
::: {.column width="58%"}

![](../img/proj-ex-annot_2025.png){fig-align="center" width="100%" fig-alt="A screenshot showing an example research project folder hierarchy."}

:::
:::

## 3. Avoid (manual) editing of data and results

- **Raw data files should never be edited** once produced
- Avoid manually editing files such as intermediate results ---
  do this with **code** instead

. . .

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: callout-tip
#### Treatment of data versus results

- _Raw data_: **read-only** (never edit the originals!) and **highly
  valuable** (make backups!)
- _Results_: essentially **disposable** -- you should be able to
  regenerate them easily
:::

## 4. Use machine- and human-readable file names

Three key principles ([Jenny Bryan](https://speakerdeck.com/jennybc/how-to-name-files)) ---
file names should be:

A) Machine-readable
B) Human-readable
C) Ordered correctly by default alphanumeric sorting

## 4a. Machine-readable names

- **Don't use spaces in file names**
- Only use: letters/numbers (<kbd>A-Za-z0-9</kbd>), underscores
  (<kbd>_</kbd>), hyphens (<kbd>-</kbd>), periods (<kbd>.</kbd>)

. . .

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

- Where appropriate, include **metadata** like sample ID, date, and
  treatment:
  - [`sample032`]{style="background-color:#C1E5F5"}`_`[`2016-05-03`]{style="background-color:#FBE3D6"}`_`[`low`]{style="background-color:#D4EDDA"}`.txt`
  - `samples_`[`soil`]{style="background-color:#C1E5F5"}`_`[`treatmentA`]{style="background-color:#FBE3D6"}`_`[`2019-01`]{style="background-color:#D4EDDA"}`.txt`

## 4b. Human-readable names

> *"Name all files to reflect their content or function.*
> *For example, use names such as `bird_count_table.csv`, `manuscript.md`,*
> *or `sightings_analysis.py`."* [@wilson2017]

. . .

One good scheme:

- Use **underscores** (<kbd>_</kbd>) to delimit units: sampleID, batch,
  treatment, date
- Use **dashes** (<kbd>-</kbd>) to delimit words within a unit:
  `grass-samples`
- Limit **periods** (<kbd>.</kbd>) to file extensions
- Generally *avoid capitals*

```bash-out
mmus001_filtered-by-mq30_sorted.bam
mmus002_filtered-by-mq30_sorted.bam
```

## 4c. Names that sort correctly

- **Dates**: write as `YYYY-MM-DD` (e.g., `2020-10-11`) --- sorts correctly
  *and* is unambiguous

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}

Sorting with the `MM-DD-YY` format:

```bash-out
TODO
```

:::
::: {.column width="45%"}

Sorting with the `YYYY-MM-DD` format:

```bash-out
TODO
```

:::
:::

## 4c. Names that sort correctly (cont.)

- **Use leading zeros**: `sample005`, not `sample5`

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
_Without leading zeros:_
```bash-out
sample1
sample10
sample11
sample2
sample3
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
_With leading zeros:_
```bash-out
sample01
sample02
sample03
...
sample10
sample11
```
:::
:::

. . .

## 4c. Names that sort correctly (cont.)

- Group similar files and number scripts by execution order:

```bash-out
DE-01_normalize.R
DE-02_test.R
preprocess-01_fastqc.sh
preprocess-02_multiqc.sh
```

# Documenting your research project {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## Why document your work?

- It's not always easy -- documenting can feel like a waste of time when
  something *then and there* seems obvious
- But you won't have a clear picture a month later, and a collaborator
  won't either

. . .

::: callout-tip
Make a **conscious effort** to take a step back, slow down, and write
down what you did and why.
:::

Code is self-documenting to a large extent -- but that shouldn't make you
complacent about documenting your work!

## Maintain README and other documentation files

Documentation should contain all information needed to reproduce your
research, e.g.:

- Where/when/how each data and metadata file originated
- Versions of software, databases, reference genomes

. . .

![](../img/proj-ex-annot_2025.png){fig-align="center" width="55%" fig-alt="An annotated screenshot of a recommended project folder hierarchy."}

## Three types of documentation files

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}

**README**\
(top-level, always!)

- Project overview
- Folder structure & file naming
- Data details
- Contact info

:::
::: {.column width="33%"}

**Lab notebook**\
(`doc/diary.md`, by date)

- What you did and why
- Not "clean" -- keep failed
  attempts too

:::
::: {.column width="33%"}

**Workflow/protocol**\
(`doc/workflow.md`, by execution order)

- Code to **rerun** final analyses
- *Should* be "clean"

:::
:::

## Use plain-text files

- We'll work almost exclusively with **plain-text** files (e.g. `.txt`)
  -- can be opened by any text editor on any computer
- Contrast with binary/proprietary formats like `.xlsx` or `.docx`

. . .

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

Plain-text files are preferable for reproducible science because they:

- Can be accessed on any computer, including remotely
- Can be operated on by Unix shell commands and any programming language
- Are future-proof
- Can be version-controlled appropriately

. . .

::: callout-tip
You'll use **Markdown** (`.md`) files -- a nice balance between ease of
writing/reading and formatting options. More on this next lecture!
:::

::: exercise
#### {{< fa comments >}} Do you have a note-keeping/documentation system? {-}

- Do you use any specialized electronic lab notebook systems?
:::

# Recap {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## Recap: Project organization & documentation

- Use **one folder** per project; separate file kinds into **consistent
  subfolders**
- Never manually edit data/results -- use **code**
- Use **machine- and human-readable** file names, sorted correctly by
  default
- Prefer **relative paths**, starting from your project's top-level dir
- Maintain a **README**, a **lab notebook**, and a **workflow/protocol**
  file, in plain text (Markdown)
